up.chip_name: tight up to constants in both directions

lo.note: Theorem 1, for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$: against the hardest input distribution, unlimited correlated samples are worth nothing. The obstruction is the [Shaltiel04] examples -- distributions with a small easy part, which many samples let you hunt for -- and the proof builds hard distributions with no easy part, via likelihood boosters: a decision tree that with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ multiplies the likelihood ratio between $D_0^k$ and $D_1^k$ by at most $M$. [BenDavidBlais20minimax] reprove it from their Shaltiel-free minimax theorems.

partial:
\(\mathrm{Corr}(f) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{R}(f)\big)\) partial Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{Corr}(f) \le \mathrm{R}(f)\)
    BDGHMT20
    Take $k = 1$: $\mathrm{Corr}_\varepsilon(f,D) \le \mathrm{D}_\varepsilon(f,D)$, and $\max_D \mathrm{D}_\varepsilon(f,D) = \mathrm{R}_\varepsilon(f)$ by Yao.
  • \(\mathrm{R}(f) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{Corr}(f)\big)\)
    BDGHMT20 BenDavidBlais20minimax
    Theorem 1, for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$: against the hardest input distribution, unlimited correlated samples are worth nothing. The obstruction is the [Shaltiel04] examples -- distributions with a small easy part, which many samples let you hunt for -- and the proof builds hard distributions with no easy part, via likelihood boosters: a decision tree that with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ multiplies the likelihood ratio between $D_0^k$ and $D_1^k$ by at most $M$. [BenDavidBlais20minimax] reprove it from their Shaltiel-free minimax theorems.

The measure is not interesting one distribution at a time -- there $\mathrm{Corr}(f,D)$ can be $O(1)$ while $\mathrm{D}(f,D) = \Omega(n)$ -- so the whole content is in the $\max_D$. That is also what makes it useful: the theorem is the ingredient that upgrades $\mathrm{R}(f\circ g) = \Omega(\mathrm{bs}(f)\mathrm{R}(g))$ to $\Omega(\mathrm{fbs}(f)\mathrm{R}(g))$, see comp-R.

see also: \(\mathrm{Corr}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Sel}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{D}^{\mu}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{fbs}(f)\), comp-R, Direct sum and direct product data/relations/04-composition.yaml

other_lo.note: A one-to-one and a two-to-one table differ in $\ge n/2$ of the $n$ cells, so every sabotaged input has $\ge n/2$ stars and a single random query finds one. [BenDavidKothari18, Sec. 1.4] give this example in exactly this role.

Not stated this way in the source, which only needs a polynomial gap, but it is
what its lemmas give. On $\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k$, Lemma 27 gives
$\mathrm{R} = \Theta(\sqrt{k\log k})$, while Theorem 3 applied to their
$O(k\log k)$ algorithm for $\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k \circ \mathrm{GapMaj}_k$ gives
$\mathrm{noisyR} = O(\log k)$. So $k = 2^{\Omega(\mathrm{noisyR})}$ and
$\mathrm{R} = \Omega(\sqrt{k})$.

params.name: eps
params.description: Error probability, over the draw of the samples.
params.dependence: Unlike single-sample distributional complexity, this model does admit cheap error reduction: $\mathrm{Corr}_\varepsilon(f, D) \le O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\delta^2)\cdot \mathrm{Corr}_{1/2-\delta}(f, D)$ (Fact 1 of [BDGHMT20]). Run the weak algorithm on fresh samples and take the majority -- which is legal precisely because all the samples come from the same side. In the single-sample setting the same trick is unavailable, and that failure is the reason $\mathrm{D}_\varepsilon(f,D)$ is so badly behaved at small bias.

facts: Theorem 1 of [BDGHMT20]: $\mathrm{Corr}(f) = \Theta(\mathrm{R}(f))$ for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$. The easy direction is $\mathrm{Corr} \le \mathrm{R}$ (take $k=1$ and apply Yao).

Against a fixed distribution the measure genuinely differs: on $\mathrm{XOR}_n$ with Shaltiel's distribution ($0U^{n-1}$ w.p. $99\%$, $1U^{n-2}0$ w.p. $1\%$) one has $\mathrm{D}(\mathrm{XOR}_n, D) = \Omega(n)$ but $\mathrm{Corr}(\mathrm{XOR}_n, D) = O(1)$ -- query the first bit of many samples until an easy one turns up.
So Theorem 1 is exactly the statement that Shaltiel examples can be avoided by choosing the distribution well, which is what makes it useful for composition.
Lemma 7 of [BDGHMT20]: $\mathrm{Corr}(f, D) = \Theta(\mathrm{biCorr}(f, D))$, the variant where the algorithm must also say which side it thinks the samples came from at every leaf.
The application: with $\mathrm{Corr} = \Theta(\mathrm{R})$ in hand, [BDGHMT20] prove $\mathrm{R}(f\circ g) = \Omega(\mathrm{fbs}(f)\mathrm{R}(g))$ -- see comp-R.
[BenDavidBlais20minimax] reprove Theorem 1 by a different route (Shaltiel-free minimax theorems), concurrently and independently.
self.name: Correlated samples complexity
self.short: Distributional complexity when the algorithm may query as many independent samples from the same side as it likes.

partial:
\(\text{Equal up to constants distribution-free, } \textbf{not} \text{ distribution by distribution}\) partial Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{Corr}(f, D) = O\big(\mathrm{Sel}(f, D)\big) \text{ for every } (f,D)\)
    BDGHMT20
    Theorem 2.1: a selection algorithm already tells you which side the samples came from, since it names an instance and its value.
  • \(\mathrm{Sel}(f) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{Corr}(f)\big)\)
    BDGHMT20
    Only after maximising over $D$: both sides are $\Theta(\mathrm{R}(f))$. There is no pointwise version -- see below.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\exists (f, D):\ \mathrm{Sel}(f, D) = \Omega(n) \text{ while } \mathrm{Corr}(f, D) = O(1)\)
    BDGHMT20
    Theorem 2.2, so selection is strictly harder at a fixed distribution. Related to this, selection admits no cheap error reduction (Theorem 2.3) while correlated samples do (Fact 1). The two facts sit either side of the $\max_D$: pointwise the measures differ by an unbounded factor, distribution-free they agree up to constants -- both being $\Theta(\mathrm{R})$. This is a good illustration of how much work $\max_D$ does in the definition of a distributional measure.
see also: \(\mathrm{Corr}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Sel}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{D}^{\mu}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), Direct sum and direct product data/relations/04-composition.yaml
